summary: Tampa Bay's entrance light: first lit 1848; the brick tower of 1857-58 still stands. Keepers until 1989 or 1990; in 1861 its lamps and oil were carried off during the war.

lens.where: lens removed 1944; 1858 third-order Fresnel lens; later beacons (per LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Second tower, first lit 1858; upper portion and lantern removed 1944
First tower (1848), replaced; not standing. Fort De Soto History says the September 1848 hurricane battered it; LighthouseFriends says it survived the storm
Assistant keeper's dwelling, built 1899 with a $3,500 appropriation; keeper's dwelling demolished 1954 (archive and LighthouseFriends)

access.note: The archive lists the station as open to the public. LighthouseFriends: owned by the Coast Guard, managed by Egmont Key State Park; grounds open, tower closed; ferry from Fort DeSoto County Park. Fort De Soto History reports the light still burns, automated and unmanned.

facts.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (National Wildlife Refuge from 1974)

events.note: Lieutenant Napoleon L. Coste recommends a light at the north point of Egmont Key
Congress grants $10,000 for a light on Egmont Key
First tower of brick: Francis A. Gibbons contract for a lighthouse and dwelling, $6,250
Tower certified 19 April 1848; first keeper Sherrod Edwards activates the light
Hurricane of 23 September 1848 covers the island with several feet of water
Congress appropriates $16,000 for a new tower (18 August 1856)
Second, taller brick tower completed roughly ninety feet inland
Third-order Fresnel lens shows a fixed light at a focal plane of 86 feet

Cutter John Appleton and steamer Cuyler cruise the island; men from the Cuyler land (thirty or forty, with three eighteen-pounders) and build a battery (Tampa Peninsular, 20 July); local guard companies remove the lamps and oil to Tampa (Richmond Whig, September)
Fourth-order lens activated 2 June 1866 after the war
Fixed red sector placed in the light (30 December 1893)
Third-order lens with two red sectors installed
Fort Dade built on the island during the Spanish-American War; deactivated 1923
New dwelling for the assistant keeper, $3,500 appropriation
Acetylene light on a reinforced concrete pile structure forms range lights with the lighthouse
Conch-shell signal replaced 18 February 1916 by a bell struck by machinery
Hurricane of 25 October 1921 (the storm of 21-26 October) damages Gulf coast aids; Egmont Key depot and light station repairs requested
Upper portion of the lighthouse and the Fresnel lens removed; rotating beacon placed on the capped tower
Remaining keeper's dwelling demolished, replaced by a one-story barracks
Egmont Key becomes a National Wildlife Refuge managed by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
Island added to the National Register of Historic Places, for the lighthouse and Fort Dade
Automated: LighthouseFriends says 1989; Fort De Soto History says the Coast Guard staffed it until 1990
Modern LED beacon replaces the DCB-24 beacon atop the tower (2018 or 2019)

corrections.why: The record's standing tower is the second tower. The 1848 brick tower was battered and replaced; LighthouseFriends dates the new tower's completion to 1857, and the archive gives its establishment year as 1858.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends says the second tower was completed in 1857 and began exhibiting its light in 1858. The archive gives 1858 as the tower's establishment year. The story uses 1857 for construction and 1858 for first lighting.

LighthouseFriends describes a conch shell sounded in answer to signals (1907 Light List). The 1916 Bulletin describes a hand horn. Both agree the signal was replaced by a bell struck by machinery in February 1916. The story reports both descriptions.

Fort De Soto History says the hurricane battered the first tower and that it was replaced; LighthouseFriends says the tower survived the storm (pile foundation credited) and that lightning later cracked it. The story reports both accounts. The replacement date (1856 appropriation) is the same in both.

notes_for_editor: Keepers: taken from the archive's place record by roster.py (107 postings, 1847-1989; 'at least' and '-' spans kept as approximate; 43 Coast Guard postings with no position stated; person slugs from the archive). The story names none of the post-1960 Coast Guard or keeper postings. LighthouseFriends' keeper list differs from the archive in places: it gives William T. Coons as one span, 1866-1876, where the archive gives two stints, and it adds Archie Clemons (1961 onward) and a few others not on the archive list. Edwards: the archive has him to 1850, LighthouseFriends says he resigned soon after the 1848 hurricane. Not resolved. Automation date: LighthouseFriends says 1989; Fort De Soto History and Wikipedia say 1990 (Wikipedia used only as a lead). Not resolved; both are cited. The 1861 events: the Richmond Whig (lamps and oil removed by local guard companies, September 1861) and the Daily Dispatch (July 1861) and the New York Herald reprint of the Tampa Peninsular (men from the Cuyler landed 30 or 40 with three eighteen-pounders and built a battery, July 1861; the Herald headline is 'federal force') are primary newspaper sources. The Dispatch item is itself a reprint of the Peninsular. The lens story (LighthouseFriends: keeper George V. Rickard took the lens to Tampa; Fort De Soto: hidden in Tampa until after the war) is not confirmed by any newspaper read here. The 1861 keeper's name is not in the Richmond paper. The 1921 storm: the Bulletin gives 25 October; the Commissioner's report gives 21-26 October 1921. The Commissioner's report does not name Egmont Key in the storm sentence; the link is its listing of Egmont Key depot and light-station work after the storm. The 1848 hurricane date (23 September) and the rope-and-palmetto story come from LighthouseFriends, which calls the rescue a local legend; Fort De Soto's rope detail was not used. Wikipedia used for leads only. The Fort De Soto History article is a local history site, not a primary source; each of its claims used here is either confirmed by a newspaper or flagged as its account. Two 1861 newspaper pages were read only in their cached OCR. The Florida State Parks history page is blocked (403) and was not read.
